title: Spot it, report it: the first minutes with a phishing message

narration: I read odd messages for a living.
Most want one thing from you.
They want you to hurry.
beats.visual_intent: the presenter at her desk, level and unhurried; the word hurry sets beside her as she says it, then the frame slides past her into an ordinary office at the end of the day

grounding.claim: phishing messages pressure you into acting before you stop to think

narration: Say this is Jo,
at the end of a long day.
A message lands.
Confirm your password within the hour,
or lose access to the shared drive.
beats.visual_intent: a drawn office at dusk, one figure at a laptop; a new message slides into the inbox and the camera pushes in until the message fills the screen, its subject line and deadline readable

grounding.claim: Jo and the message are invented
a short deadline or threat of losing something is the urgency sign
a request for a password is a sign

narration: Act now, it says.
Jo's cursor is already on the link.
You have been here too.
beats.visual_intent: the cursor drifts across the message and settles on the link; everything freezes mid-motion and the frame holds still for a beat of silence

grounding.claim: the moment of choice is invented

narration: You will read this message for what it is,
know the one move that beats it,
and what to do after a click.
beats.visual_intent: the frozen message stays dimmed behind; three short anchors set one by one in the open space beside it

grounding.claim: the lesson's promise

narration: You already glance at sender and subject.
This is not ten more tips.
Just four moves, for the message that says hurry.
beats.visual_intent: the frozen message shrinks back into a full, ordinary inbox; a long imagined list of tips fans out and folds away, leaving one empty frame for four items

grounding.claim: the lesson gives four behaviours, not a list of tips
grounding.source_anchor: brief must_cover (from_user): the requester's four behaviours

narration: Phishing, in one line.
Criminals send a message
to get you to open a link or attachment,
give away a password,
or send money.
beats.visual_intent: the word phishing set large over the dimmed message; three small marks appear on the message itself as each aim is named: the link, the password box, a payment line

grounding.claim: phishing tries to get you to open a harmful link or attachment, give away information such as a password, or send money

narration: Move one,
look for the signs.
Move two,
do not click it, or reply to it.
beats.visual_intent: the four moves in large plain type, set one by one over the dimmed frozen message, which never leaves the frame

grounding.claim: look for the signs
grounding.source_anchor: brief must_cover (from_user): the requester's four behaviours

grounding.claim: if you suspect phishing, do not click its links, open its attachments or reply

narration: Move three,
report it with your company's report button or channel.
Move four, the one people skip,
if you already clicked, report it at once,
and do not hide it.
beats.visual_intent: moves three and four join the first two; the fourth sits a little apart, with a quiet mark of emphasis

grounding.claim: report it with the company's report button or channel
grounding.source_anchor: brief must_cover (from_user): the requester's four behaviours

grounding.claim: if you have already clicked, contact your IT or security team and tell them what happened

narration: Why move three matters.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre, the NCSC,
has a case study from one financial company.
beats.visual_intent: the four moves slide aside, move three stays lit; an empty funnel draws in, with a small office block at its mouth labelled as one company

grounding.claim: an NCSC case study describes a financial company

narration: 1,800 phishing emails arrived.
The filters stopped 1,750 of them.
That left 50,
in staff inboxes.
beats.visual_intent: a counter at the top of the funnel reads 1,800 as the emails pour in; the filter layer catches them and the counter drains to 50 as 1,750 fall away; the 50 land as small envelopes in a row of inboxes

grounding.claim: the company received 1,800 phishing emails; filtering stopped 1,750, leaving 50 in staff inboxes

narration: Filters catch most. Not all.
Staff reported 25 of those 50,
with a report button.
Some of them after clicking.
beats.visual_intent: among the 50 envelopes, 25 small report marks light up one after another; a few of them carry a small click mark first

grounding.claim: staff reported 25 of those emails with a report button, some after clicking

narration: Those reports were the first sign
the attack had got past the filters.
beats.visual_intent: the 25 lights travel back up out of the inboxes to the security team's desk, arriving before anything else signals the problem

grounding.claim: those reports were the first sign the attack had got past the filters

narration: An early warning, for everyone else.
The sooner the team knows,
the more harm it can limit.
One company, mind, not a general rate.
beats.visual_intent: the security desk lights up and a calm ring spreads out from it across the other inboxes in the building

grounding.claim: reports act as an early warning for everyone
knowing sooner lets an organisation limit the harm
one company's incident, not a general rate

narration: Filters catch most,
reports catch what gets through.
Which move got those 25 to the team?
Move three, report it.
beats.visual_intent: the funnel shrinks to a small icon in the corner and the frozen message from the opening returns to centre

grounding.claim: filtering stopped most of the emails
staff reports were the first sign

recall.prompt: Which of the four moves put those 25 reports in front of the security team?

narration: You may have learned to spot bad spelling.
Plenty of old scams were sloppy.
This one is written perfectly.
beats.visual_intent: the camera pushes back into Jo's message; a magnifier passes over it looking for typos and finds none, each line ticks clean

grounding.claim: some phishing messages are now written perfectly

beats.misconception: You can spot phishing by bad spelling, clumsy grammar or a strange logo.

narration: Spelling is no longer a reliable sign.
Some phishing fools even experts.
Look at what it wants from you.
beats.visual_intent: the magnifier sets down; a plain label beside the message reads spelling, not reliable, and the message stays clean and convincing

grounding.claim: bad spelling and grammar are no longer a reliable sign; some fool even experts

narration: First, what is it pushing you to do?
Within the hour, or lose access.
That pressure is doing the work.
Its job is to stop you checking.
beats.visual_intent: the message held still; the deadline line lifts off it as a marked callout labelled pressure, and stays pinned on the board beside the message

grounding.claim: phishing pressures you into acting before you think
a short deadline or threat is the urgency sign

narration: It also claims to be IT support.
Phishing likes to borrow authority.
Reason enough for you to look twice.
beats.visual_intent: the sender name lifts off as a second callout, authority, pinned under pressure; the two together form the pressure family

grounding.claim: phishing often pretends to come from a trusted or important person or organisation, so authority deserves a second look
the IT support sender name is invented

narration: Now slow down.
The name says IT support.
The address has one letter changed.
beats.visual_intent: the camera closes on the address; the real spelling slides in beneath it and the one changed letter lights up, everything else grey

grounding.claim: a sender address that does not match the real one, such as one letter changed, is a sign

narration: Then the link.
It is shortened, so it hides where it goes.
So you have the mismatch sign,
not who, or where, it claims to be.
beats.visual_intent: the short link unfolds into its full destination, which is plainly not the shared drive; it lifts off as a callout and joins the address under the label mismatch

grounding.claim: a shortened link that hides where it goes is a sign

narration: Last, what does it want from you?
Your password, the request sign.
Banks and other official sources
do not ask for this by email.
beats.visual_intent: the password box lifts off as the last callout, request; Jo's inbox has now become an evidence board with three families pinned around one clean message

grounding.claim: a request for a password or bank details is a sign; banks and official sources do not ask for this by email

narration: Pressure, mismatch, request,
three kinds of sign, one clean message.
Your move stays the same,
do not click, report it.
beats.visual_intent: the three family labels brighten in turn on the evidence board, then the message dims and the two moves set over it

grounding.claim: urgency, mismatch and requests for credentials are signs
mismatched sender or link
password requests
do not click or reply

narration: Here is the part people miss.
A name you know can still be fake.
beats.visual_intent: the evidence board slides away and a new message arrives in the same inbox, from a familiar contact with a known avatar

grounding.claim: targeted phishing can seem to come from a known colleague, manager or supplier

narration: Say your usual supplier, Quillmoor Supplies, writes.
Please pay today's invoice,
to our new bank details.
Plus an attachment nobody expected.
beats.visual_intent: the supplier message held on screen, its name and logo familiar, the attachment icon at the bottom, nothing marked yet

grounding.claim: Quillmoor Supplies and its message are invented

narration: The name is familiar, and that is the point.
Targeted phishing uses what it knows
about a company and its people.
See if you can find the three signs.
beats.visual_intent: the familiar name glows softly; the rest of the message waits unmarked while the viewer looks

grounding.claim: targeted phishing uses information about a company and its people to look convincing

recall.prompt: Pressure, mismatch, request: which can you find before they are marked?

narration: Today is the pressure.
New bank details, the payment request,
and that unexpected attachment.
Most work attachments are genuine,
so unexpected is what makes you check.
beats.visual_intent: the three signs mark themselves on the supplier message in the order spoken: the word today, the bank details, the attachment

grounding.claim: urgency is a sign
a request for financial information is a sign
an attachment you were not expecting is a reason to stop and check; most attachments at work are genuine

narration: If it might be genuine, check it,
by a route you find yourself,
not the number or link in the message.
Then report it.
beats.visual_intent: beside the message, a separate path draws out to the supplier's contact found in the company's own records, bypassing the link and number in the message

grounding.claim: check through a separate route you find yourself, not the link, number or address in the message

narration: The same ask,
as an email, a text, a chat message.
Only the channel changes, so your move does not.
beats.visual_intent: the supplier email re-forms as a phone text, then as a chat bubble, side by side; the same three sign marks line up across all three while only the channel changes

grounding.claim: phishing also arrives as text messages, chat messages and phone calls

narration: One aside.
In phishing simulations,
the median click rate for text or voice
was 40 percent higher than for email.
Simulations, and relative to email.
beats.visual_intent: a small, quiet label sits under the text and chat bubbles: in simulations, 40% higher than email; no headline, no alarm

grounding.claim: in phishing simulations, the median click rate for text or voice was 40% higher than for email

narration: You do not need to be sure.
If it feels off, do not act.
Report it, and let the team look.
beats.visual_intent: the three channels settle into one row and a single report mark lands on each

grounding.claim: do not click or reply to a suspected phishing message
report it with the company's report button or channel
grounding.source_anchor: brief must_cover (from_user): the requester's four behaviours

narration: Remember the funnel.
Some of those 25 reports came after a click.
This story goes there.
beats.visual_intent: a brief glimpse of the funnel with its 25 lights, then a slow dip to a new time and a different desk

grounding.claim: some of the 25 reports came after clicking

recall.prompt: Some of those 25 reports came from people who had already clicked.

narration: Say this is Ravi, earlier in the week.
Back to back meetings, a delivery notice,
and he clicked before he noticed.
That happens to busy people.
beats.visual_intent: a second drawn figure between meetings, laptop half open; a delivery notice, a click, and the screen carries on as if nothing changed

grounding.claim: Ravi and the delivery notice are invented
people click for many reasons, including being busy and stressed

narration: Nothing seemed to happen.
The tempting thought:
I typed nothing, why tell anyone?
beats.visual_intent: Ravi pauses with a small thought bubble holding the tempting line; the frame stays soft and unhurried

grounding.claim: Ravi's thought is invented
people who fear blame stop reporting their mistakes

beats.misconception: If I clicked but typed nothing, there is no need to tell anyone, and keeping quiet is safer for me.

narration: From the click, two paths.
On one, Ravi quietly deletes it.
The team learns nothing.
beats.visual_intent: from the click the frame splits in two; on the left path the message is deleted and the early-warning light from the funnel flickers at Ravi's desk and never travels to the security team

grounding.claim: reports are the security team's early warning

narration: On the other, he reports it at once,
through your company's report button or channel,
and says what he clicked.
The warning arrives,
in time to limit the harm.
beats.visual_intent: on the right path a report goes out, the light travels to the security desk and arrives, and Ravi's screen settles into a calm handled state

grounding.claim: if you clicked, contact your IT or security team and tell them what happened
reports including after clicking act as an early warning
knowing sooner lets an organisation limit harm

narration: Blaming people for clicks does not work.
People who fear blame stop reporting.
If you click, no panic.
Tell the team.
beats.visual_intent: the split resolves to the right-hand path only; Ravi back at his desk, the day carrying on, nothing dramatic

grounding.claim: blaming people who click does not work; people who fear blame stop reporting
do not panic; tell your IT or security team what happened

narration: Clicked is not the end of it.
Quiet is.
Report it now, and say what you clicked.
beats.visual_intent: move four from the opening list returns, large and plain, over Ravi's settled desk

grounding.claim: if you already clicked, tell your IT or security team what happened
if you already clicked, report immediately and do not hide it
grounding.source_anchor: brief must_cover (from_user): the requester's four behaviours

narration: Your turn.
Say a colleague's chat message says,
sign in to this shared document within the hour,
or the edits are lost.
A, click to see if it is real.
B, reply in the chat and ask.
C, report it, without clicking.
D, delete it and move on.
Your first move? Pause, and decide.
on_screen: A: click to see if it is real
B: reply in the chat and ask
D: delete it and move on
beats.visual_intent: a fresh chat message on screen, the question above and four option cards as peers below it, then a real silent pause

grounding.claim: the chat message is invented
urgency is a sign
a request to sign in, meaning a password, is a sign

recall.question: First move?
options: A: click to see if it is real
B: reply in the chat and ask
D: delete it and move on
recall.why: the deadline is pressure and sign in means your password behind a link; report it without clicking or replying
recall.tempting_wrong: B feels polite, but the reply goes to whoever controls the account; D protects you but the team never gets its early warning

narration: It is C.
The hour is pressure,
and sign in means your password, behind a link.
B feels polite,
but your reply goes to whoever controls that account.
D keeps you safe,
but the team gets no warning.
Unsure? Ask them by a separate route.
on_screen: B: reply goes to the account
beats.visual_intent: card C lifts and the two signs mark themselves on the chat message; then B and D each get one plain line on why they fall short, while A stays grey

grounding.claim: urgency is a sign
a request for a password is a sign
do not reply to a suspected phishing message
check through a separate route you find yourself
reports are an early warning for everyone

narration: Back to Jo's message:
within the hour, one letter off,
a shortened link, a password.
So, what does Jo do?
beats.visual_intent: the opening dusk office and Jo's frozen message return; the four signs mark themselves on it in quick succession, then the frame holds for the viewer to answer

grounding.claim: urgency sign
mismatched sender or link
password request

narration: Jo does not click.
Jo reports it,
with the company's report button or channel.
The afternoon carries on.
beats.visual_intent: the cursor moves off the link to the report control; the message folds away into a calm handled state and the office settles, no celebration

grounding.claim: do not click
report it with the company's report button or channel
grounding.source_anchor: brief must_cover (from_user): the requester's four behaviours

narration: Had Jo clicked,
reporting at once still protects everyone.
Today, find your company's report button or channel.
Hurry is the sign. Reporting is the move.
beats.visual_intent: the presenter returns, level and dry; the pocket rule sets beside her in two lines

grounding.claim: reports, including after clicking, are an early warning for everyone
find where the report button or channel sits
